children: US asset manager BlackRock will divert up to $100 billion of its international capital deployment to the Middle East, focusing on sectors such as infrastructure and opportunities arising from the opening of state-owned assets to private markets, BlackRock told Zawya.

“The GCC is equipped with a reasonably solid balance sheet position, but at the margin, our analysis suggests that we are going to see something like $100 billion in capital that may have flowed out is going to stay here,” said Ben Powell, Chief Investment Strategist for the Middle East and APAC — BlackRock Investment Institute, while referring to the GCC “an investment destination for global allocators of capital”.

Powell, though, dismissed a sense of urgency in deploying this capital in a region that has been significantly impacted by ongoing escalations in the near seven-month US-Iran conflict, calling it more of an opportunity than a necessity, coupled with investors also pulling back a “little bit” from the US market in recent months.

“While US Treasuries are still obviously a very important asset and will play an important role in global portfolios, at the margin there has been diversification in the fixed income sleeve into private credits, more emerging market bonds and so forth,” Powell said, adding: “With that in mind, more of that capital is going to stay at home and be deployed domestically by asset allocators.”

The evolving role of sovereigns in the region, along with a broader investor base and changes in investment opportunities are the driving factors behind this flip in capital outflow, according to the $15.3 trillion asset management behemoth. The UAE already witnessing two such take-private deals in 2026 with L’IMAD’s acquisition of the Abu Dhabi National Energy Company (TAQA) in August, followed by its tender offer to raise its stake in AD Ports Group to over 98.5% earlier this month. Though Blackrock was not part of these deals, on Tuesday its infrastructure investment firm Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) signed a deal with Qatar’s Lesha Bank to invest more than $1 billion in projects.

“Sovereigns have historically been capital allocators, but what we are also seeing is them turning into market architects that are reshaping the dynamics, either by working with regulators to attract international companies or asset managers or forming partnerships as global managers or anchoring funds to invest in the local economies,” said Ayman Daif, Managing Director, Head of Aladdin Business Development for the Middle East, Central Asia, Africa and India, BlackRock.
New York-based BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, manages more than $175 billion in the Middle East.

Fundraising in the region, which has largely been dominated by Saudi Arabia and the UAE, has also seen a decisive shift based on asset class, BlackRock said. Though the real estate sector raised $4.2 billion in 2021, it fell to $0.1 billion last year. Private equity moved the other way: from $0.1 billion in 2015 to $4.5 billion so far in 2026.

While Saudi Arabia is rapidly closing the gap between international and domestic dealmaking, privatisation and monetisation across the energy, utilities and water sectors are creating opportunities in the GCC that suit both mid-market and large-scale strategies, the asset manager said, citing growing investment opportunities in infrastructure, pipelines, data centres and other high-quality large-scale assets across the region.

GCC states will invest about $2.1 trillion by 2030, with spending focused on making economies more resilient to disruptions in trade, shipping and energy markets, according to BlackRock Investment Institute.

Middle East sovereign wealth funds indicated a 43% allocation of their exposure to private capital, compared with 35% for their rest-of-world peers. The share of Middle East LP investors positive on or considering private equity mandates has climbed from 70% in 2019 to 83% in 2026, BlackRock said it in a report titled Market Evolution: The Middle East.
(Reporting by Bindu Rai, editing by Seban Scaria)

title: BlackRock to divert up to $100bln toward GCC’s infrastructure, wealth fund opportunities
